synopsis: This accepted preprint contributes a claim-level evaluation method and author-reported results from one paper-derived computational research task. For pieces 01–03, its evidentiary role is to inform delegation boundaries, show how submitted artifacts can be checked against explicit criteria, and expose resource and reproducibility constraints. The authors report that only 14 of 90 end-to-end claims met their criteria, while stagewise runs supplied with paper-derived inputs performed better. These are bounded benchmark findings, not independently verified model rankings or autonomous discoveries. Orientation here does not replace passage citations for later substantive claims.
limitations_and_counterevidence: The study uses one SPINT-derived task and an LLM judge with researcher spot-checking, rather than exhaustive independent validation. Its authors evaluate their own framework; independent replication is not established by the supplied text. Stagewise improvements and better writing with skills qualify a uniformly negative reading. Comparisons also involve unequal instruction coverage and different hosts. Test sessions could inform optimization, and private FALCON evaluation was not used. Paper-derived rubrics may undervalue valid alternatives, and pretraining exposure remains possible. Resource figures describe time and tokens, not monetary cost or causal efficiency gains. The source provides a repository link, but extraction does not verify its contents or reproducibility. These orientation notes require supporting passages before use as substantive synthesis claims.

passages.purpose: Verification method and human oversight (§3.3): evidence-linked ratings, a specified LLM judge, researcher spot-checking, and integrity gates. Supports treating human review as a safeguard without asserting that judge bias occurred.

locator.quote: LLM judge. We use an LLM as the judge, with claude-opus-5 as the evaluator model. Each stage is judged in its own call. In each call, the judge reads the rubric together with the reference entries its items cite. It also reads the frozen submission and the upstream artifacts visible to that stage. For each item it returns an integer rating on a 0–4 scale with item-specific anchors, along with the locations of the supporting evidence and a short rationale. Every score can therefore be traced back to evidence. A domain researcher spot-checked the judge’s ratings and rationales and found them largely consistent with their own assessment. Integrity gates guard the ratings against contaminated evidence, such as leaked reference content or fabricated execution, by setting the items that depend on it to zero (Table [12](#A5.T12) in Appendix [E](#A5)).

passages.purpose: Principal reported result (Appendix G): preserves the distinction between method claims and empirical claims, preventing the total met count from being presented as 14 successful empirical findings.

locator.quote: Of the 90 end-to-end claims, 14 are met, and E5 for GPT-6 Astra is the only empirical claim met in an end-to-end run.

passages.purpose: Delegation comparison and counterevidence (§5.1): supplying reference-derived upstream inputs improved performance; the authors' upstream-error explanation is an interpretation of that comparison.

locator.quote: At every stage, all three harnesses score higher in stagewise runs than in end-to-end runs. The gains are largest in experimental execution and results analysis. Within execution, most of the gain comes from result quality and claim completion rather than code execution, and the number of claims that meet their success criteria rises from one to three in end-to-end runs to seven or eight in stagewise runs (Table [16](#A7.T16) in Appendix [G](#A7)). Much of the end-to-end execution gap thus appears to originate upstream of execution.

passages.purpose: Reported skill comparison and self-report discrepancy (§5.3): includes improved writing alongside weaker execution and the gap between reported success and adjudicated attainment.

locator.quote: ARIS and Orchestra reach overview scores within one point of Codex alone (44.5 and 45.2 vs. 45.1), but this parity hides a trade-off. They score 15.0 to 20.0 points higher on paper writing (52.5 and 47.5 vs. 32.5), yet lower in execution, where result quality drops from 30.0 to 20.0 for both and claim completion from 42.5 to 32.5 and 37.5. Each also reports success on eight claims within half an hour of starting execution but meets only one criterion (Figures [4](#S5.F4)a and [4](#S5.F4)b).

passages.purpose: Comparison qualification and human intervention (Appendix A): instructions were developed through human-directed pilots, and orchestration systems did not receive identical instruction coverage.

locator.quote: The workspace instructions were revised over several rounds of pilot runs and frozen before any scored run. Table [7](#A1.T7) lists the four revisions with the pilot behavior or rule gap that motivated each and the file that states it. The five general-purpose harness runs received byte-identical instructions with all four revisions. The skill-augmented harnesses received the same instructions with one added line that invokes their skills. The research-orchestration systems receive the stage instructions through their own entry points. They therefore carry the first two revisions but not the stage order in TASK.md or the initial-instruction line on background experiments.

passages.purpose: Nominal compute budget (§4.3): grounds practical resource planning while distinguishing allowed resources from actual consumption and monetary cost.

locator.quote: Resources and budgets. Every run receives one GPU with 32 GB of memory and the task data. The required packages are preinstalled in a configured execution environment. An end-to-end run has 72 hours of wall-clock time, and a stagewise run receives a separate time budget for each stage, from 2 hours for the claims stage to 48 hours for experimental execution (Table [3](#A1.T3) in Appendix [A](#A1)). We impose no token limit (resource use in Table [13](#A6.T13) in Appendix [F](#A6)).

passages.purpose: Resource counterevidence (§5.4): preserves the expensive low-scoring exception and the authors' qualification that larger resource use does not guarantee better results.

locator.quote: The main exception is DeepScientist, which runs for 7.0 hours and uses the most tokens of any system (205.7 M), yet scores only 39.9. More resources thus accompany higher scores on average but do not guarantee them.

passages.purpose: Test validity and deployment boundaries (Appendix B): optimization could use test sessions; local scores cannot establish private-leaderboard performance, and offline latency cannot establish closed-loop deployment.

locator.quote: Train, validation, and test sessions may all be used while optimizing a claim. Every test access must be logged with its purpose, configuration, and result, and test results that informed optimization may not be described as untouched or unbiased estimates. Calibration to a new session may read its neural activity but not its behavior labels, and it may not update model parameters. The primary metric is per-session multi-output variance-weighted \(R^{2}\), with negative values preserved. Because the sessions are selected locally from the public data, these scores are not comparable to the private FALCON leaderboard. Latency is processing time divided by the duration of the decoded data. A ratio below one is an offline result, not evidence of closed-loop deployment.

passages.purpose: Author-acknowledged limitations (§6): preserves alternative-method bias, possible pretraining exposure, and the planned rather than completed extension to additional anchor papers.

locator.quote: Our study also has limitations. Because the rubrics follow the anchor paper, they may undervalue scientifically valid alternatives to its design. In addition, the literature cutoff restricts what a system can retrieve during a run but does not rule out exposure to the anchor paper during pretraining. In future work, we will apply ResearchFlow-Eval to additional autoresearch systems, models, and anchor papers.

passages.purpose: Reproducibility gap in evaluation (Appendix E): model pinning does not supply judge seeds, temperature control, repeated samples, or uncertainty estimates from repeated judging.

locator.quote: All ratings come from claude-opus-5, called through the Claude Code CLI with the model pinned. Each call draws one sample, with no fallback model and no selection or averaging across samples. Temperature and seed are not exposed by the interface.
